title: Publishing the third year of digital verification inclusion data

content.content: This week we published our third annual report on inclusion in the certified digital verification services (DVS) market. The report helps to monitor inclusion and accessibility in the certified digital identity market over time. This year's report shows continued progress on accessibility, alongside some barriers that still need to be addressed. You can read the full report on GOV.UK.

Digital verification services can help people access services by proving their identity or other information about themselves online. These services must be accessible and inclusive to ensure that all people can benefit from them. The Office for Digital Identities and Attributes monitors inclusion across the certified DVS market to understand where providers are making progress, where barriers remain, and where government action may be needed.
How we monitor inclusion

Services certified against the UK digital verification services trust framework must complete an annual inclusion monitoring survey. This year, 44 organisations across the certified digital verification services market completed the survey.

The survey covers areas including documentation and evidence, accessibility, biometric verification, data collection, and user support. Responses are anonymous and individual organisations are not assessed. Instead, we combine the responses to build an overall picture of inclusion and accessibility across certified digital verification services.
Previous years' reports can be found below:
Key findings
The findings show continued progress in several areas:
Cost and limited alternatives remain barriers
While the overall picture is positive, organisations continue to report barriers to improving inclusion.

Cost remains the most reported barrier, with a majority (61%) identifying the cost of implementing inclusive features as a key challenge, up from 50% in 2025. A significant minority (34%) also identified limited access to government-held data as a barrier, down from 48% in 2025.

Alternatives to biometric verification also remain limited. Of the 44 organisations surveyed, 39 reported using biometric technology as part of their service. Around half of those organisations offer another route for people who cannot or do not wish to provide biometric information.

Vouching remains uncommon. Vouching is a process where a person formally confirms someone else’s identity. It can help people who do not have traditional identity documents access digital verification services. Three organisations reported offering vouching, but none currently have a vouching route within the scope of their certification. Organisations identified fraud concerns and reluctance among relying parties (organisations accepting identity checks) as the main barriers to wider use.
What have we learned from three years of monitoring?

This is now the third year of inclusion monitoring, allowing us to build a clearer picture of trends across the certified DVS market. The findings show where progress is being made and where further work is needed.

The findings also show that inclusion cannot be understood through a single measure. Accessibility features and standards are important. So are alternative ways to complete an identity check, information about where users encounter difficulties, and evidence about whether services work for diverse groups. We will use these findings to inform our future policy work and ensure that anyone who chooses to use a digital identity can do so.
Read the 2026 inclusion monitoring report on GOV.UK.

title: From messy data to meaningful connections: Introducing Splink 5

content.content: We are excited to introduce Splink 5, the latest version of the Ministry of Justice's open-source software for linking records across datasets.
Developed to tackle some of government's most complex data-linking challenges, Splink has grown into a tool used across the UK public sector and around the world.

Across large organisations, information about the same person can be spread across multiple systems, duplicated, incomplete or inconsistent. Connecting those records accurately is essential for delivering better services, better research and better decision-making.
That's where Splink comes in.

Splink helps organisations identify records that belong to the same person or entity, even when the underlying data is messy or inconsistent. For example, someone's name may be spelled differently across two systems, they may have changed address, or one record may contain a typo.

While this might sound like a niche challenge, it is something almost every large organisation encounters. Accurately linking records improves data quality, reduces duplication and helps organisations make better use of their data.
That's one reason Splink has seen substantial adoption across the public sector, with more than 22 million downloads and use across at least 10 central government departments and agencies.
What Splink 5 brings to the table
Splink 5 is our biggest step forward yet, making it easier to link data at a scale that was previously difficult or impossible for many organisations.

The new release can handle substantially larger datasets and is now one of the fastest linkage engines in the world. In our testing, Splink linked a billion records in less than 10 minutes, helping organisations turn vast amounts of data into meaningful insights more quickly than ever
Detailed release notes for Splink users can be found here
Impact across the justice system

Within the Ministry of Justice, Splink plays a vital role in bringing together information from courts, prisons and probation services. By connecting data that would otherwise remain fragmented across multiple systems, it helps create a more complete understanding of people's interactions with the justice system.

The technology powers JustLink and supports the Data First research programme, enabling richer analysis of court outcomes, offending patterns and journeys through the justice system. It also sits at the heart of Core Person Record and is beginning to give frontline prison and probation officers more timely and accurate linked data.
A home-grown tool with a global footprint
Built to solve justice-system challenges, Splink is now delivering impact far beyond the Ministry of Justice and is used widely
Recent use cases include:
The Australian Bureau of Statistics won a public sector award for their work using Splink to build the 2025 National Linkage Spine
Try it out for yourself
Splink 5 is entirely free, open source, and available to anyone right now.

What started as a solution to some of the Ministry of Justice's most complex data-linking challenges is now helping organisations across government, academia and beyond connect data with greater accuracy and confidence.
From supporting justice services to enabling research around the world, Splink is helping organisations turn messy data into meaningful connections.

title: Two nations, one rising tide: how the Environment Agency and the Netherlands work together to keep communities safe
authors: Caroline Douglass, Exec Director of Flood and Coastal Risk Management

content.content: Water doesn't respect borders. Neither does the expertise needed to manage it.

This month, we welcomed colleagues from Rijkswaterstaat, the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management's executive agency to England, bringing together two organisations that manage some of the world's most significant flood and water challenges.
It's a timely moment for this kind of exchange. As we mark Flood Action Week, we're asking people across England to think about their own flood risk and what they can do to prepare.

Meeting with our Dutch counterparts is a reminder that the same thinking applies at a much larger scale: none of us can manage the pressures of a changing climate alone, and we all stand to benefit from sharing what we've learned.

Discussions focused on common challenges including ageing infrastructure, asset management, workforce capability and long-term resilience. Most importantly, they reinforced a shared commitment to continued collaboration and practical action that benefits the communities we serve.
Why this matters now

Climate change is not waiting for anyone. Rainfall is becoming more intense, sea levels are rising, and coastal communities across the world are adapting to a future that looks different from the past. No single organisation has all the answers. But by pooling our knowledge with organisations globally, we get closer to the solutions communities need.

We are all adapting to more extreme weather, managing ageing infrastructure and working to build resilience for future generations. By learning from one another and sharing expertise openly, we can move further and faster than we could alone.
Built on people, not paperwork

These aren’t partnerships that live in a filing cabinet. They are sustained through regular engagement between senior leaders, technical specialists swapping notes on real projects, and joint learning activities that put people from both organisations in the same room, tackling the same problems.

That matters because flood risk management isn't theoretical. It's about whether a family's home stays dry. Whether a business can keep trading after a storm. Whether a coastal town has time to prepare before the water arrives.

The relationships we build with organisations like Rijkswaterstaat translate directly into better decisions here in England on crucial topics from maintaining critical assets and developing future skills to strengthening our long-term planning for climate resilience.
What we've learned, and what's next
We don't claim to have solved flood risk. No one has. But we can say, with confidence, that we are better equipped to face it because of our partnerships.

The recent visit from Rijkswaterstaat reaffirmed that there is enormous value in these relationships. While our organisations may operate in different countries the challenges facing England and the Netherlands are remarkably similar.

Furthermore, we are united by a common purpose: protecting people, places and livelihoods from the impacts of flooding and coastal change. That shared purpose will continue to guide our work together in the years ahead because the challenges of flooding and coastal change don't stop at a coastline or a border.
Protecting people from flooding is core to what we do. Partnerships like this one help us do it better, but we also need your help.
Find out more about how you can protect your home or business this Flood Action Week by visiting www.gov.uk/flood-action.

title: Join our  FluSurvey  programme and contribute to protecting the nation’s health this winter

content.content: Our scientists are tracking influenza (flu) and other respiratory viruses and they need your help. Join our FluSurvey UK-wide citizen science programme and contribute directly to protecting the nation’s health this winter.

When you register for FluSurvey, you'll be invited to report any respiratory symptoms on our website on a weekly basis. It’s quick and easy to submit the information, and you’ll be playing a part in protecting the health of all of us across the country. You’ll also be able to track your symptoms on your profile each week. We’d also encourage you to share the link with your friends and family - the more of us who participate, the better the data will be.

At points during this winter season, some eligible adults with respiratory symptoms who live in England may also be invited to take part in PCR testing as part of our preparedness and surveillance activities.

We are ramping up our comprehensive surveillance systems to monitor flu and other seasonal respiratory viruses over the winter season, and FluSurvey is one of the key methods we use to understand how these viruses are spreading in our communities. This is valuable information for us because not everyone who feels unwell will call 111, visit their GP, or go to hospital, so their symptoms may not be captured. Community-based systems like FluSurvey include data from those who manage their symptoms at home, giving us an early understanding of respiratory illness activity across the whole population. FluSurvey metrics are also presented on our award-winning UKHSA data dashboard, which shares public health data in a simple, inclusive and accessible way.

When added to our existing sources of information, the value of real-time data on respiratory illnesses, provided directly by people across the country, is immense. It's like having thousands of health detectives scattered across the country, all working together to build a comprehensive picture of flu-like illnesses. By taking part in FluSurvey, you would be contributing a vital piece to a larger puzzle.
If you’re interested in taking part, sign up for FluSurvey today.

title: Progressing SFI26 applications from Windows 1 and 2

content.content: In this blog, we give an update on the nearly 19,000 applications received during Windows 1 and 2 of the SFI26 offer.
It also confirms arrangements for Window 2 exception groups.
Progress on agreement offers
The Rural Payments Agency (RPA) continues to process applications as quickly and efficiently as possible.
We received around 6,700 applications in Window 1. Of these, we’ve issued roughly 6,600 agreement offers, of which 95% have now started.
Of the approximately 12,200 applications received in Window 2, the RPA has issued around 2,500 agreement offers so far. Roughly 36% of these agreement offers are now live.

Applications are usually processed in the order in which they were submitted. Some applications require additional checks and can therefore take longer to process. However, processing is progressing well overall.
SFI26 Window 2 ‘exception groups’
Previously, we said we would allow two small ‘exception groups’, who contacted the RPA before Window 2 closed, to continue with their applications, as follows:
Given the short Window 2 application period, Ministers have decided to extend the ‘technical issue’ exception group to include:
Farmers who reported issues after 11:59pm on 29 September will not qualify for the extended technical issue exception group.
This is a targeted response to the specific set of circumstances for Window 2. It does not set a precedent for how we will approach exception groups in future.
The RPA is continuing to work through queries received from farmers and agents as quickly as possible. This includes assessing reports of technical issues. This may take a few more weeks to complete.

Some farmers and agents have reported that a technical issue prevented them from applying for SFI actions on 22 September which they expected to be available. However, in many of these cases, the system correctly prevented them from applying for combinations of ineligible actions.

Where, following assessment, the RPA finds that this is the case, these SFI26 applications will not be considered as a technical issue exception. This will similarly be the case for queries without sufficient supporting evidence for the RPA to confirm that there was a valid technical issue.
Following assessment, the RPA will write to farmers and agents to confirm whether they are considered to be in an exception group or not.

We are continuing our close work with farmers and stakeholders to look at how we can improve SFI for next year. As part of this, we are exploring alternatives to a first come, first served application process for SFI in 2027.
Funding available through Higher Tier
Farmers can still apply for Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT) funding via the Expression of Interest (EOI) process.
You can submit EOIs for woodland improvement and agroforestry, as well as new single-focus agreements for management of species rich grassland and scheduled monument management.

title: How Derbyshire County Council successfully transitioned 250 schools to the DfE's Risk Protection Arrangement (RPA)
authors: Hazel Coates, Insurance Manager, Derbyshire County Council

content.content: Hazel Coates from Corporate Services and Transformation at Derbyshire County Council, shares how her local authority realised greater benefits for schools and saved over £600,000 by switching to RPA.
Reasons for change

For years, Derbyshire County Council provided insurance cover for around 450 schools through a pooled approach. This system worked well  by combining all schools together, the Council could negotiate better rates and give every school comprehensive protection, even if some didn't need all the cover included.
However, as more schools became academies over the years, the pool shrank from 450 schools to around 250.

With fewer schools contributing to the insurance fund, competition from the DfEs Risk Protection Arrangement (RPA) – the departments alternative to commercial insurance, and the rising cost and complexity of cyber cover meant the Council could no longer offer the same value.

When Derbyshire County Council compared their existing school insurance with the RPA, it wasn't just comparable,  it was actually better in key areas, especially for cyber protection and at a significantly lower cost per pupil.
This led to a clear decision: all remaining council-maintained schools in Derbyshire would transition to the RPA.
Keys to success

Schools particularly valued how both the council and DfE handled the administrative burden. Rather than each school navigating complex insurance changes individually, they managed the work together , including bulk enrolment, registering all schools in one go.

The result has been overwhelmingly positive feedback from schools about what proved to be a largely seamless transition. Schools could focus on educating children while benefiting from insurance that's both comprehensive and cost-effective.
Benefits for our schools
Transition to the RPA offers several significant advantages for Derbyshire schools:
Wider benefits

The move to the RPA has allowed the Council to redirect resources previously used to subsidise school insurance towards delivering its other major statutory responsibilities for adult and children’s social care, highways and public health.
Transferring schools to the RPA has enabled the Council to substantially reduce the cost of its insurance premiums and to halve its insurance excess for property.

Importantly, Derbyshire County Council maintains its responsibility towards education and continues to work with schools on various aspects of risk management. For example, during severe weather events or flooding, the Council will still work collaboratively with schools, the Environment Agency, and other stakeholders to provide support, regardless of whether they're RPA members.
Its role has simply shifted from being the insurance provider to being a partner in risk mitigation and support.
In summary, the transition to the RPA has been a positive experience for both Derbyshire schools and the Council, made significantly easier by the excellent support provided by the DfE.
The move reflects the Council’s commitment to finding the best value and most appropriate solutions for our schools, even when that means stepping back from services it traditionally provided.
Act now

This was purely a ‘business decision’. The Council always prides itself on the service it gives to schools, and which is highly valued by them. It’s about ensuring our schools have access to the most cost-effective and suitable arrangements in an ever-changing educational landscape.
If your local authority hasn't yet explored the RPA, start conversations now. The potential savings and improved coverage could significantly benefit your school's budget and protection.
The RPA represents a sustainable, cost-effective approach to school insurance that benefits both schools and local authorities.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this blog were provided by Derbyshire County Council and reflect its specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: NHSE Home Test Alpha Assessment

content.content: From: DHSCAssessment date: 30/04/2026Stage: Alpha assessmentResult: GreenService provider: NHSE
Service description

This service aims to solve the problem of enabling people to order clinically approved home testing kits through a national digital platform, integrated with the NHS App. The service supports discreet, accessible testing outside of traditional clinical settings, starting with HIV self‑testing and designed to scale to additional test types in future. Users can order a test, receive clear guidance on how to complete it, return samples where required, and receive results with appropriate follow‑up information and signposting to care. The service is designed to improve access, equity and public health outcomes while supporting local authorities and suppliers through a consistent national platform.
Service users
Initial HIV use case
Scalable multi-test platform
Report contents
1. Understand users and their needs
Decision
The service was rated green for point 1 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:

The panel was impressed that the team actively sought out inexperienced testers and marginalised users through community pop-up research sessions rather than relying solely on standard recruitment. We liked that the team used this research to create visual step-by-step guides that support people with reading difficulties and those for whom English is a second language.
2. Solve a whole problem for users
Decision
The service was rated green for point 2 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service

The panel was impressed that the team took a mature, systemic view to solve a whole problem by clearly mapping the boundaries between the NHS App, third-party test suppliers, and local clinical pathways. We liked that the team applied rigorous data minimisation by stripping identifiable information from the results API payload to reduce data leakage risks across systems.
3. Provide a joined-up experience across all channels
Decision
The service was rated green for point 3 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service

The panel was impressed that the team simulated parallel offline touchpoints, such as physical testing kits and promotional posters, alongside the digital prototypes during research sessions. We liked that the team established a clear operational split for user support, where NHS England handles pre-order queries and test suppliers handle post-order queries.
4. Make the service simple to use
Decision
The service was rated green for point 4 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service

The panel was impressed that the team streamlined the ordering flow to reduce cognitive load. The panel liked that the team removed confusing intermediate pages and reframed address collection around eligibility to make the process quick and straightforward. The panel was impressed that the team made a strategic decision in making best use of their resources to follow the “fail fast and fix it” principle during alpha.
5. Make sure everyone can use the service
Decision
The service was rated green for point 5 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service

The panel was impressed that the team embedded an accessibility auditor in the team and reviewed production code at an accessibility lab to identify structural improvements. We liked that the team used plain language and avoided medical jargon to ensure the service is inclusive for people with low health literacy.
6. Have a multidisciplinary team
Decision
The service was rated green for point 6 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
7. Use agile ways of working
Decision
The service was rated green for point 7 of the Standard.
8. Iterate and improve frequently
Decision
The service was rated green for point 8 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:

The panel was impressed that the team uses highly iterative, user-centred design cycles to quickly evolve the service. The panel liked that the team not only tested their designs, but actively retested new iterations with the exact same user groups to confidently validate that their changes worked. A great example of this was when they identified that users with reading difficulties were overwhelmed by the start page, and then successfully proved their redesigned, simplified page resolved the issue.
9. Create a secure service which protects users’ privacy
Decision
The service was rated green for point 9 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
10. Define what success looks like and publish performance data
Decision
The service was rated green for point 10 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
11. Choose the right tools and technology
Decision
The service was rated green for point 11 of the Standard.
12. Make new source code open
Decision
The service was rated green for point 12 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
13. Use and contribute to open standards, common components and patterns
Decision
The service was rated green for point 13 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:

The panel liked that the team built the service using established, accessible patterns from the NHS App and GOV.UK design systems to reduce cognitive load and provide a familiar experience. The panel was impressed that the team rigorously tracked pattern reuse in their page evolution history, successfully borrowing proven elements from parallel services like Digital Health Checks and the Hepatitis C home testing journey.
14. Operate a reliable service
Decision
The service was rated green for point 14 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:

The panel was impressed that the technical architecture uses intelligent decoupling (such as Amazon SQS queues) to prevent orders from being lost if a third-party supplier goes offline. We liked that the team has proactively mapped out unhappy paths - such as unreturned kits, insufficient blood samples, and API drops - and acknowledged the need to tackle these carefully.
Next Steps
Green - alpha
This service can now move into a private beta phase, subject to getting approval from the CDDO spend control team. The service must meet the standard at beta assessment before launching public beta.

title: What is severe drought?

content.content: Drought is tightening its grip on England

On 15 October 2026, Severe drought status was declared for parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex after the driest April to September in over a century depleted local reservoir levels - with further dry weather expected for the rest of October.

This summer was exceptionally hot and dry, with record temperatures and prolonged periods of low rainfall. These conditions have continued into autumn, placing significant pressure on water across the country. The usual seasonal rainfall has yet to arrive, and 82% of England remains in drought.

As a result, several reservoirs are at exceptionally low levels for this time of year. To recover in some areas, we need 120% of typical rainfall over the next six months. Without it, drought conditions will continue and could worsen.

Without sufficient autumn rainfall and continued intervention measures, there is an increasing risk to water supplies. Given the seriousness of the situation and the potential impact on essential water resources, severe drought status has now been declared in parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.
What is severe drought?

Severe drought is the highest level of drought that can be declared. It’s declared when our evidence shows drought is causing, or will soon cause, serious harm, and that emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services.
What does a severe drought declaration mean?
Exceptional action is now needed to conserve water and protect public supplies.

Severe drought doesn't automatically trigger restrictions, and it isn't a civil emergency. But it is serious. It means government and other organisations step up their response together, acting where it matters most to reduce harm and support recovery. It gives everyone involved a shared, evidence-based understanding of how serious things are, so we can coordinate more effectively
What does severe drought mean for the public?

Severe drought doesn't automatically mean new restrictions. But in areas affected, your water company may introduce further water-saving measures to protect supply. This could include taking more water from the environment, limiting some business use, supply interruptions, or reducing mains pressure. Your water company will contact you directly if this affects you.

You can help protect water supplies too. Small changes at home and at work make a real difference: taking shorter showers, fixing leaks, using water carefully in the garden, using the eco-setting on dishwashers and washing machines, avoiding pre-rinsing dishes before loading the dishwasher, fitting a low-flow shower head, using a Cistern Displacement Device, filling washing machines to their recommended load, installing a water butt, and turning off taps when brushing teeth. These aren't token gestures. They cut the amount of water we need to take from rivers and groundwater, protecting supplies for people and leaving more for wildlife, wetlands and the natural systems we all depend on.
The choices we make about water, in drought and beyond, help protect England's rivers, wetlands and wildlife for the future.
Find out more on how to save water.
Why have only certain areas declared severe drought?

We've declared severe drought where public water supply is most at risk:  around Ardingly in West Sussex and Wimbleball in Somerset. The severe drought declaration covers the homes and businesses served by these two reservoirs.
Check with your water company to find out if you're affected.
What is the Environment Agency doing to protect water supplies?

We are working closely with Defra and the affected water companies to protect water supplies during these exceptional circumstances. This includes an enhanced incident response, increased monitoring and reporting, supportive communications and continuing to regulate companies.

We're increasing our scrutiny of water companies to make sure they stick to their statutory drought plans. That means more monitoring, more checks, and faster processing of permit applications, so we can protect public water supplies while safeguarding the environment and local wildlife.

Given the exceptional circumstances, in close discussion with the Government, the Environment Agency is using its regulatory discretion to give priority to protecting public water supply in specified severe drought areas when exercising its relevant functions.
How does the Environment Agency support severe drought declaration?

Science underpins everything we do to manage water resources and prepare for climate change. It tells us what's happening now, flags emerging risks, and shapes how we plan ahead. Most importantly, it turns evidence into action.

Our scientists and hydrologists monitor rainfall, river flows, groundwater levels and reservoir storage across England every day. This evidence shows us how drought is developing and what it means for people, water supplies and the environment.

We work with water companies, government, farmers and environmental groups to agree practical steps: closer monitoring of vulnerable rivers and habitats, promoting water efficiency, and managing water resources carefully through dry periods.

We share this evidence with partners through the National Drought Group and regional drought groups, so we can respond to changing conditions in real time. It shapes decisions on drought status and wider government action, and helps us identify where wildlife and habitats are under the greatest pressure.
Science is not something that happens alongside decision-making; it absolutely underpins how we regulate, the advice we provide and the actions we take.
What happens next?
Until enough rain brings recovery, we will not hesitate to take the action needed to protect water supplies.
We continue to monitor conditions closely, working with partners and the government to reduce the impact of severe drought to communities and the environment.

title: Ebola: what are the symptoms and how does it spread?

content.content: Ebola has been in the news since the World Health Organization's declaration of a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May 2026, for an outbreak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. This blog post outlines what the disease is, how it spreads, and what it means for the UK.
What is Ebola?

Ebola disease is caused by a group of viruses known as orthoebolaviruses. It affects both humans and animals, and was first identified in 1976 during near-simultaneous outbreaks in Zaire, now the DRC, and Sudan, now South Sudan.

Between 1979 and 1994, no human cases were reported. Since then, outbreaks have occurred with increasing frequency, including a large West Africa outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which caused over 28,000 reported cases and saw intense transmission in urban areas for the first time. Several countries, including the UK, reported imported cases linked to that outbreak.

Four species of the virus are known to cause disease in humans, alongside a fifth found only in animals so far, and a sixth discovered specifically in bats in 2018, whose potential to infect humans is still unknown.
What is the risk for the UK?

The current outbreak poses a low risk to the UK population. Imported cases are extremely rare, and only 4 confirmed cases have been reported in the UK since 1976, and there have been no UK deaths from the disease. The NHS has established procedures and specialist centres for managing any suspected cases.
How do you catch Ebola?

Ebola spreads through close contact. Person-to-person transmission happens through contact with the body fluids of someone who is infected, sick or has died from the disease, or through contact with contaminated objects such as needles or soiled clothing.

In rarer cases, people become infected through contact with infected animals, such as bats or non-human primates, in countries where the virus is present. Fruit bats are believed to be the natural reservoir for the virus: a species where the virus can live, grow, and multiply.

Importantly, an infected person can only spread the virus once symptoms begin. There's no evidence that Ebola spreads through intact skin, or through coughing or sneezing, in the way that flu or COVID-19 does. The virus can also persist in certain parts of the body, including the testes, eyes and central nervous system, after someone has recovered, and transmission through sexual contact with a survivor has been documented, with the virus detectable in semen for over a year.
What are the symptoms?

Symptoms usually appear suddenly, between 2 and 21 days after infection, with an average of 8 to 10 days. Early symptoms are flu-like: high temperature, extreme tiredness, muscle aches, sore throat and headache.

These are often followed a few days later by vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach pain. Some people go on to develop a rash, cough, shortness of breath, red eyes, bruising, and yellowing of the skin and eyes. In more severe cases, bleeding can occur as the disease progresses. This may include blood in poo and bleeding from different parts of the body.

Because early symptoms are non-specific, diagnosis can be difficult, and cases are sometimes mistaken for malaria, typhoid or meningitis in the early stages. Laboratory testing, carried out under high-level biological containment, is needed to confirm infection.
How serious is Ebola?

Ebola is rare but can be fatal. The average case fatality rate is around 50%, though this has ranged from 25% to 90% in past outbreaks, depending on the virus species and other factors, including patients' age and access to care.
Can it be treated?

There's no specific cure, but patients require intensive supportive care, including fluids and help maintaining blood pressure and oxygen levels. Two monoclonal antibody treatments are available for Ebola caused by the Zaire virus species, the strain responsible for most major outbreaks, though there are currently no licensed treatments for other species.
Is there an Ebola vaccine?

Two vaccines are licensed to help prevent infection from the Zaire virus. One is given as a single dose and can be used to respond quickly during an outbreak. The other requires 2 doses given 8 weeks apart, so is less suited to emergency response but can still play a role in prevention. Neither vaccine is currently effective against the Sudan virus species, though vaccines for this strain are in development.

Preventing spread relies heavily on strict infection control. Patients need to be isolated, and healthcare workers and carers need to use appropriate protective equipment, since procedures like handling blood or inserting intravenous lines carry particular risk. The bodies of those who have died from Ebola remain highly infectious and must be safely buried or cremated.
What is UKHSA’s role in Ebola outbreaks?

UKHSA is responsible for protecting the UK from health threats like Ebola. This means monitoring outbreaks overseas, assessing risk to the UK, and coordinating the public health response when needed. UKHSA also works with the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO), the Department for Transport (DfT) and Border Force, so that travellers returning from affected areas know what to do if they develop symptoms. We also provide testing through the NHS for anyone who becomes unwell after travelling to an affected region.

The UK Public Health Rapid Support Team (UK-PHRST) helps low- and middle-income countries respond to infectious disease outbreaks. The team was established after the 2014 to 2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak and funded by the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC). To date, the team has delivered both in-person and remote deployments to support World Health Organization (WHO), both in WHO headquarters and country offices in DRC, the Republic of the Congo and South Sudan. We have offered technical expertise across a range of disciplines including infection prevention and control, epidemiology, risk communication and community engagement, data modelling and readiness training at both country and regional levels.
The deployments follow formal requests for assistance through the Global Outbreak Alert and Response Network, with UK-PHRST working alongside WHO, UNICEF and partners throughout.

The DHSC-funded, UKHSA-delivered International Health Regulations Strengthening Project (IHR-SP) is supporting the Ebola response within our partner countries and across the region. We’ve helped the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention establish an expert advisory cell to guide strategy, and by strengthening cross-border surveillance and coordination in higher-risk countries, including an agreement between Uganda and South Sudan to improve health security collaboration. The response has shown the value of embedding UKHSA experts within African institutions from the outset of an emergency, providing immediate, trusted support while building longer-term regional health security capacity.
Where can I find out more?
There is a dedicated page on GOV.UK that lists outbreaks and case locations of haemorrhagic fevers Ebola and Marburg.

content.content: Be a part of history by naming the UK’s Active Debris Removal Mission, the UK Space Agency’s first ever national space mission.
The UK is leading the way in space sustainability, taking action to clean up our orbital environment.

Currently, satellites are thrown away after they stop working, sometimes for the simplest of reasons; like running out of fuel! This has led to an increasingly cluttered and potentially dangerous space environment.
New technologies are being developed to allow the repair or removal of broken and old satellites. We want your help to name our pioneering Active Debris Removal Mission.
If your mission name is selected, you will be making history by naming the ADR Mission and you will see the name etched on the side of a spacecraft!
Our competition is easy to enter and closes on Thursday 10 December 2026.

The UK Space Agency is launching its first national space mission to tackle the growing threat of space debris. This marks a pivotal step in the UK’s efforts to protect vital space technology and ensure the long-term safety of the Earth’s orbit.

A special spacecraft built by ClearSpace UK with advanced British technology will fly into space and grab two old satellites that no longer work. It will gently guide them back towards Earth, where they will safely burn up in the atmosphere, helping to keep space clean and protecting the remaining satellites that we rely on every day for things like maps on our phones.
Learn more about the ADR Mission.

Space missions are often given memorable names that help people connect with and understand their purpose. Inspired by exploration, discovery, science and mythology, these names become an important part of a mission's identity and legacy.

title: What can a small flatfish tell us about pollution in our seas?

content.content: For more than three decades, a small flatfish in the UK has been helping scientists investigate some difficult questions: is pollution in the marine environment getting better or worse, and does it have an impact on the marine life that lives there? Sudden pollution incidents such as oil spills do unfortunately occur from time-to-time, which can have a devastating impact on marine life. However, there are also teams of UK scientists dedicated to investigating the long-term environmental impacts of human activities, specifically concerning chemicals that we have become dependent on in our day-to-day lives.

The common dab (Limanda limanda) flatfish is not a species known for attracting public attention, but for marine scientists, dab have long played an important role as a sentinel species that can help reveal the biological effects of marine pollution. In a newly published study in Environment International, Cefas scientists examined long-term trends in liver tumours in dab collected from 29 monitoring sites from five biogeographical marine regions in the UK. The results showed a significant decrease in the overall prevalence of these tumours over time, providing encouraging evidence that the biological effects of hazardous chemicals may have reduced in parts of the UK marine environment. However, the story is not simply one of recovery. While the study shows that things appear to be moving in the right direction, liver tumour prevalence remains high in some areas, particularly parts of the Irish Sea and North Sea, despite the observed decrease. Understanding why these patterns persist is now an important scientific and policy question.
Why do scientists investigate liver tumours in fish?

The liver is one of the main organs responsible for the processing and excretion of chemicals. In fish, as in other animals, it can show abnormal tissue changes (pathology) which can provide evidence of exposure to harmful substances. Certain liver pathologies, including tumours, have been used for many years in marine monitoring programmes as indicators of biological effects associated with chemical exposure. This does not mean that every tumour has a simple or single cause. Marine environments are complex, and fish are exposed to many natural and human pressures throughout their lives. But when patterns are observed consistently across time, location and age groups, they can provide important clues about the health of the wider environment.
A long-term investigation

This is one of the largest studies ever conducted to investigate long-term trends in liver tumours in fish and their potential causes. Linking chemical exposure to biological effects in wildlife is notoriously difficult and relies on the consistent long-term collection of baseline monitoring data. The value of monitoring is often only fully realised after many years, when the time series becomes long enough to reveal patterns that would otherwise remain hidden. One of the strengths of this Cefas study is the length and consistency of the offshore surveys that underpinned this work, conducted under the Clean Seas Environmental Monitoring Programme (CSEMP) on board the RV Cefas Endeavour. This is the UK government’s principal monitoring programme for understanding the health of our seas by bringing together chemical measurements in sediments and fish with biological effects data, including liver pathology. It has been established for several decades monitoring approximately 29 locations from five biogeographic marine regions around the UK including the Northern North Sea, Southern North Sea, Irish Sea, Eastern Channel, and Western Channel and Celtic Sea. The integrated approach of CSEMP allows scientists to look beyond the presence of contaminants alone and assess whether chemical pressures are associated with measurable effects in marine wildlife. Each fish represents a small piece of evidence including where it was collected, how old it was, how large it was, and what liver pathology was seen under the microscope. Individually, those observations tell us relatively little. However, when thousands of observations are brought together across years and locations, they become a powerful dataset. This allows scientists to determine whether disease patterns are changing, whether some marine regions are more affected than others, and whether environmental improvements are being reflected in the health of wild fish.
Encouraging signs, but questions remain

The overall decrease in liver tumour prevalence is an encouraging finding that may reflect the benefits of improved regulation and reductions in some hazardous chemical inputs into the marine environment. However, the higher prevalence of tumours in parts of the Irish and North Seas suggests that some areas may still be adversely affected by additional pressures, including historical contamination and/or continuing inputs. Furthermore, whilst improved regulation may be a contributing factor to the observed reduction in prevalence, scientists are still uncertain about which chemicals are responsible for dab liver tumour formation in UK waters. The Cefas study showed that concentrations in dab livers of a now banned and highly persistent family of chemicals, the Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs), were correlated with higher incidences of liver tumours, although the team treated this finding cautiously. While it was interesting to observe this correlation, as scientists we need to be cautious regarding what our data show, because correlation does not always mean causality. On closer examination, this relationship may partly reflect the spatial structure of the dataset. Specifically, compared with other marine regions, the higher number of sampling sites, and by extension higher numbers of fish, in the Irish Sea was considered likely to heavily influence the observed correlation.

So, could another family of chemicals be involved in causing liver tumours in dab? This is where the investigation becomes both interesting and challenging. In North America, a wealth of studies have pointed towards the Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs), as important contributors to liver tumours in several fish species. However, these studies typically focused on species sampled in relatively shallow inshore habitats where environmental contaminants are generally more concentrated. In the Cefas study, the focus was mostly at offshore locations, where measured sediment contaminant concentrations were typically lower. However, dab may not spend their whole lives in the same place.

There are several observations that provide additional clues to the possible causes of liver tumours in dab. Unlike some infections that result in acute clinical signs of disease, carcinogenesis is generally a chronic process, with tumours developing over an extended period. Our data also show that liver tumours are rarely observed in dab younger than three years of age. Together, these observations suggest that the events initiating carcinogenesis may occur considerably earlier in life, well before tumours become detectable. This is particularly interesting because many marine fish can spend their early life in coastal and inshore habitats before moving farther offshore as they mature. Taken together, the evidence supports the hypothesis that dab may be exposed to hazardous chemicals closer inshore and at a much younger age, with the resulting tumours only becoming apparent later, once the fish have moved offshore. In other words, the tumours observed in offshore dab may be evidence of earlier exposure, but their location does not necessarily tell us where that exposure occurred.
Following the exposure pathway

The latest Cefas study published in Environment International was the result of monitoring that helps inform the UK’s progress towards Good Environmental Status under the UK Marine Strategy Regulations. The next step is a period of complementary research to better understand where and when exposure occurs, and which chemicals or chemical groups are most likely to be involved. We are about to embark on a four-year research project funded by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Marine and Fisheries Research & Development Commission to investigate whether trace element and isotope analysis of otoliths, the ear bones of fish, can reveal more about the life history and origins of dab, and ultimately the chemicals they may have been exposed to. This R&D matters because marine policy and management depend on knowing not only that biological effects are occurring, but also what pressures are driving them and what can be done about it. Identifying exposure pathways could help improve future monitoring, strengthen understanding of contaminant sources, and support more effective action to protect marine ecosystems.
The common dab may be a somewhat modest flatfish, but it has been telling an important story about pollution, recovery, and the continuing need to follow the evidence.

title: Lessons from steering a speedboat: what leading the Manage People on Probation service taught me

content.content: As Women in Tech Week is being marked across government and the wider community, I have been reflecting on my own experiences of leading digital transformation in a complex environment. Over the past year, I have had the privilege of serving as Service Owner for Manage People on Probation (MPOP), helping to take a new service from an early pilot to national rollout. As I prepared to move on to my next role, I wanted to share some of the lessons I have learned about leadership, delivery and transformation.

Manage People on Probation (MPOP) is a new digital service from Probation Digital that provides a single view of people on probation, helping probation staff manage individuals under their supervision, complete tasks, and record case activity more efficiently and effectively. MPOP provides time savings and quality improvements at scale, by making high-volume, everyday tasks simpler and quicker to complete.

Early in 2025, Probation Digital was gearing up to respond to growing capacity pressure  in HMPPS, and MPOP was identified as a major potential time-saver for practitioners. The Ministry of Justice also defined our delivery into two kinds: speedboats, which are faster pilots and proofs of concept, and tankers, which are slower transformations of our core systems. MPOP was described as a speedboat and an exemplar, and was set to go live nationally within 12 months. I joined as Service Owner to mature the delivery model and accelerate the rollout. I relied on a steering group of senior leaders who were deeply bought into the vision, and a multi-disciplinary team that worked and deployed alongside our probation users.
Today, MPOP is live nationally, adoption has reached nearly 90% of the target cohort, which is made up of probation practitioners with a caseload, and the team has tripled in size.
I wanted to share my reflections on what it’s like to steer a speedboat and what makes it different from other products. This is what I learned.
Building around what practitioners needed most

MPOP was in Alpha when I joined the team. The team’s hypothesis was that we could help practitioners find the information they need to make effective decisions, reduce re-keying across systems, and join up the journey between them. In a pilot of 20 users, practitioners told us they wouldn't adopt another tool in an already crowded space unless it let them do more. We pivoted by rebuilding the roadmap around the highest-volume tasks practitioners did, and moving to a multi-squad model to deliver features in parallel.
Lesson 1: Scaling should happen alongside delivery

We didn't have the luxury of slow and steady governance gates deciding and assuring whether and when we can launch the service. Our challenge was that we were going to be live with all users within 12 months. To de-risk that timescale, I thought that the safest approach was to scale consistently alongside the building work.

After the initial pilot with 20 users, we onboarded 200 more practitioners to test our early product decisions at a larger scale. We tested our scalability by growing to 700 users and more challenges started coming up - the product load times increased as more people logged in, and we also started seeing the data quirks from the legacy estate that appeared when more people had their casework exposed through the new interface.

Onboarding at least one team from each of the 12 probation regions also meant we can test if the journeys work within the regional variances of practice. A big-bang launch would have shown us all that, but on a national scale with the whole organisation watching, so our decision to roll out steadily proved useful.
Lesson 2: The most complex feature shouldn’t set the pace

We knew early on that non-compliant appointments and contacts will be complex features. They required longer discoveries and more iterations. In order to continue speedily releasing value to users at the earliest opportunity we intentionally decided to not include them as our first set of functionality.

There were plenty of other high-volume, high-value features we could work on – we know practitioners schedule multiple appointments throughout their day and record a very high volume of contacts that require no further action. We shipped those journeys first and we added some “delighters” to them to add value, such as automation with practitioners' Outlook calendars, and SMS notifications for people on probation.

With a speedboat like MPOP it was crucial that different parts of the service moved at a different pace. This helped us ensure that we’re not bottle-necked behind complexity, and that we can ship value with the simpler features upfront.
Lesson 3: A speedboat can’t do everything

The benefits of speedboats mean that we can take people to their destination really quickly! But a speedboat was never intended to move the large complex infrastructure that is required for the future.

Behind the scenes, MPOP still reads and writes to NDelius, the legacy system and database that all probation staff use, which also means that our transformation and blue-sky thinking was limited by the current shape of the technology estate. Our scaled live service performance also demonstrated that the organisation needs larger, and more in-depth transformation of the data domains and core processes to support the new ambitious products in Probation Digital.

Approximately 6 months into scaling MPOP we kicked off additional work to address the foundations and technical architecture of Probation Digital. The Probation Digital Services platform is now responsible for moving the data, creating common capability, reporting and reference, and to unify the journey across services. I intentionally set that programme of work to be bigger and slower, with a 3-year roadmap and multiple dependencies.
Leading this takes optimism and what comes next

Transformation requires optimism. If you ever find yourself in charge of a speedboat, those three points above are my advice for you. We face many challenges and constraints - established ways of working and habits that are hard to break, a highly pressurised workforce, and a policy landscape that shifts constantly. My favourite descriptions of the complex work we do in digital government is "just a cold, dark night on the side of Everest". Nobody who signs up to climb Everest thinks it will be easy.

The platform is the next chapter, and the team building it will continue that story. It's a different kind of delivery: bigger and deliberately foundational, and it will require different lessons that I can’t wait to hear about.

title: Working together sustains Hen Harrier numbers in 2026

content.content: By Matt Heard, National Delivery Director

Hen Harriers are one of the UK’s most distinctive birds of prey and, after decades of decline, have gradually returned to northern England as their population has recovered. Natural England and its partners are working to support this recovery through the Joint Action Plan, helping to balance conservation with wider land management priorities. Annual monitoring shows a long-term positive trend, with efforts focused on tracking breeding success across England. This blog gives the latest figures for 2026.
Numbers of nesting Hen Harriers in England increased in 2026, according to data collected by Natural England, RSPB and partners.

Hen Harriers are a charismatic yet elusive bird of prey species, at home on upland moorland landscapes in the UK. Once reduced to just a few isolated pockets, Hen Harriers have spread from Scotland and returned to the north of England as their numbers have gradually recovered over the past few decades.

Conflicting land management priorities have slowed their recovery, but Natural England and partners have been working to secure their future in England through cooperation under the Joint action plan to increase the English hen harrier population, which was published by Defra in 2016.

Securing a future for the Hen Harrier in England is one of the ways in which Natural England is working to deliver our latest strategy: Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, strengthening the resilience of England's ecosystems and the services they provide through the protection and recovery of key ecosystem components, including species like the Hen Harrier.
Monitoring the recovery of hen harriers in England

As part of the Joint Action Plan, Natural England and partners including the RSPB and raptor monitoring groups collect data on the number of breeding Hen Harriers each year, and, where possible, the number of chicks that successfully fledge each year. It is unlikely that all the breeding Hen Harriers in England are counted, but great effort is made to work with landowners and managers to ensure as many as possible are added to the records to give the best estimate each year. While the data collected by Natural England and partners does not always show an increase on the preceding year, the overall trend of the species' population has shown much growth on a longer timescale, in both number and distribution. Previous annual reporting on the national population, published by Natural England, can be seen here: 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022.
Breeding figures and regional breakdown

In 2026, Natural England, RSPB and partners recorded a total of 45 breeding attempts in England (39 in 2025), of which 33 were successful (33 in 2025), fledging 112 chicks (106 in 2025). This gives an average of 3.4 chicks per successful nest (3.2 in 2025).
We recorded 1 second breeding attempt in 2026. Therefore, it is estimated that there was a minimum of 44 breeding females in England (39 in 2025).
Trends in Hen Harrier numbers

The overall figures show a steady increase in breeding attempts by Hen Harriers over the past 2 years, following a crash in 2024. Anecdotal observations by field staff reported an increase in the availability of prey items (including voles) in 2026, which is likely to have contributed to this increase. However, this was not the case in all areas and a number of factors will also have played an influential role. Annual population fluctuations are to be expected for any species of wild animal, but while the national population remains so small the ability for a population to recover from a decline is significantly reduced. This highlights the need for continued effort to increase the number of Hen Harriers in England and improve their resilience to bounce back from poorer breeding years, which can result from variables such as prey and habitat availability, which may in turn be affected by land management regimes and a changing climate.

This year only 9 of the 45 recorded breeding attempts were made on moors managed for grouse in England, with the remainder across other moorland and water catchment locations (including but not limited to nature reserves). The relatively small number of breeding attempts on grouse moors could be due to the reduced monitoring of grouse moors in 2026 in comparison to previous years. Our monitoring team would welcome the opportunity to work with more moorland owners and agree access and monitoring agreements, with the aim of getting a more complete picture of Hen Harrier numbers.
Working with partners is key

We are grateful for the efforts of our partners to monitor, protect and manage Hen Harrier nests and breeding habitats. We work closely with RSPB staff who record the nesting attempts on RSPB reserves, and on the United Utilities Estate in Bowland. We are also grateful for the contributions of volunteer Raptor Study Groups and Natural England volunteers to nest monitoring, and to landowners and agencies including Forestry England, National Parks, National Landscapes, the National Trust, NatureScot and Natural Resources Wales.  Natural England field staff lead on liaison with privately-owned grouse shooting estates, and we extend our gratitude to those land managers who are encouraging Hen Harriers to nest successfully alongside their wider estate management for grouse and other wildlife.

2026 marks 30 years of consolidated data for Hen Harrier breeding activity in England. Natural England is committed to recovering nature, and the Hen Harrier is one example of how long-term dedication can have real meaningful impact for species and landscapes.
We are committed to continue to work with all partners and communities to improve the long-term recovery of Hen Harriers.

title: Organic Action Plan for England published today

content.content: Published today, the Organic Action Plan for England (OAPE) sets out how government and the organic sector will work together from 2026 to 2036 and beyond, to grow domestic production, improve market opportunities and help more people understand what organic farming offers.

Publication of the plan is the next step in the delivery of government’s ‘Farming Roadmap 2050: Growing England’s Future’. The Farming Roadmap acknowledges the vital role that organic systems play in improving soil health, cutting chemical and synthetic inputs, and supporting biodiversity.
Organic farming is a whole-farm approach that can help farm businesses reduce their exposure to input costs, such as artificial fertiliser and pesticides, and reach markets where demand is growing.
It can also support healthier soils, cleaner water, more wildlife and high standards of animal welfare.

Defra-funded research shows strong links between organic farming and benefits for biodiversity, soil health and reduced chemical exposure. It also shows how organic systems can support climate adaptation.

Consumer demand for organic products continues to grow. UK organic retail sales reached £3.9 billion in 2025. The plan aims to support English farmers to fulfil a greater share of this growing market, with an ambition to increase the proportion of agricultural land farmed organically from around 3.4% towards 10% by 2036.

Organic food plays an important role in public procurement. Produce qualifies under the Higher Environmental Production Standards within the Government Buying Standards for Food and Catering Services. Programmes such as Food for Life Served Here show what can already be achieved, with 22 catering providers spending £7.5 million on organic produce in 2024.
There’s a strong opportunity for English farmers, growers and food businesses to expand domestic production.
In this post, we look at how government and industry action - aligned with the themes and outcomes in the plan - will help encourage more farmers to convert to an organic farming system.
Purpose of the plan

Defra has collaborated with the English Organic Forum (EOF), a group of organic organisations that work together to represent the sector, to develop a plan that responds to the sector’s needs, with direct input from organic producers and sector leaders across the country. Defra and the EOF will jointly oversee its delivery.
The plan is primarily focused on England, but some actions will involve partners across the UK. It's a 10-year plan but includes action that will stretch beyond 2036.

The OAPE recognises that organic farming is not the right choice for every farm but, for some businesses, organic production can offer a stronger route to market and lower exposure to some input costs.
The plan sets out a clear pathway to grow England's organic sector and create more opportunities across the supply chain.
For farmers and growers, it aims to provide better access to information, advice, innovation and peer support, making it easier to start or expand organic production.
For businesses, it seeks to improve understanding of where domestic supply can meet demand, helping producers, processors and buyers identify new market opportunities.
For consumers and public sector buyers, it aims to increase awareness of organic certification and encourage greater uptake of English organic produce.
What this means for farmers and growers

The plan is designed to sit alongside existing agri-environment schemes (AES). Since 2024, the Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) has included options for organic conversion and maintenance. As committed in the first year of the plan, Defra will maintain and clearly explain the organic offer within Environmental Land Management (ELM) schemes for farmers considering organic conversion.

In order to grow organic production, the OAPE focuses on actions that break down other barriers to farmers converting to an organic farming system. This includes access to information, advice, peer networks, markets and supply chains.

The English Organic Forum and the wider sector will build on existing services so farmers considering conversion can find information on certification, funding, business planning and routes to market.
The sector will also work to provide one-to-one guidance and learning between farmers.

Further work will identify opportunities in horticulture, arable, dairy, red meat and poultry. Opportunities will be underpinned by better data on organic production, trade and purchasing, so farm businesses can make decisions using clearer evidence.
Case studies
We have spoken with two farm businesses about their experiences of working within an organic farming system:
Riverford Organic Farmers

Riverford Organic Farmers began in 1986. Guy Singh-Watson started growing organic vegetables on three acres at Wash Farm in Devon. The company has since grown from the UK’s first organic veg box into a business with over £100m annual turnover, delivering directly to around 70,000 customers each week.
They became employee-owned in 2018, with 100% of the business now held in an Employee Trust for the equal benefit of its approximately 1,000 employees.
Certified organic since 1989, they grow and sell food without artificial pesticides or fertilisers, GM ingredients, routine antibiotics, or artificial preservatives and colours.

Organic farming supports Riverford’s long-term resilience. Improving soil fertility, biodiversity, carbon and water storage helps the farm cope with increasing floods and drought and maintains productivity levels. It also underpins the business’s commercial identity, giving customers confidence that their food is produced to clear, trusted and independently certified organic standards.
Riverford’s principal route to market is its organic box scheme, with 70% of box contents grown in the UK and produce delivered directly from farm to customer.

The business has long-term partnerships with growers across the country, supported through its Supplier Charter, which commits to agreed prices and volumes, accepts cosmetically imperfect produce and promotes collaborative solutions when crops vary.
Riverford also works with their farmers to assess and improve performance across soil health, water, biodiversity, carbon, animal welfare and social impact.
Shimpling Park Farm

Shimpling Park Farm, owned and run by John, Alice and Rufus Pawsey, is a 700-hectare mixed organic farm near Bury St Edmunds in Suffolk, managed as a whole-farm organic system and certified by the Soil Association.

The farm grows combinable crops including milling oats, spelt, heritage wheat, quinoa, chia and lentils, alongside herbal and fertility leys. Around 200 New Zealand Romney sheep graze two-year grass-and-clover leys, integrating livestock with the arable rotation.

The organic mixed-farming system links crops, leys and livestock to build fertility and reduce reliance on external inputs. Grass, clover, legumes and herbal leys support soil health and biodiversity, while sheep turn forage into a saleable product and contribute to the rotation. As part of their system, roughly 90 hectares of leguminous and herbal leys help build soil health, biodiversity and nature.

On-farm trials also help the business identify practical approaches that can maintain yields while strengthening nature and long-term resilience. The team trials different seed rates, weed and disease controls, bi-cropping, green manures and undersowing to improve crop production while enhancing the environment.
A diverse crop base, local flour milling, building rentals and other activities provide diversified income streams.
The Shimpling team have an open and collaborative approach welcoming many people to their farm for wider connection and learning.

The farm uses Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) and Countryside Stewardship scheme funding to focus on landscape restoration, farmland birds and education. It is also participating in a Landscape Recovery pilot through the Suffolk Wool Towns cluster, which aims to connect ancient and secondary woodlands across 20,000 hectares. Earlier Countryside Stewardship funding supported pond restoration, the restoration of two medieval moated sites and medieval wood pasture, hedge replanting, and coppicing of ancient woodland.

We’ll also post a blog about future funding opportunities for farmers to convert to an organic farming system.

title: Direct consumer enforcement: 18 months on

content.content: We are now just over halfway through the second year of the Competition and Markets Authority’s (CMA) direct consumer enforcement regime under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (DMCC Act).

Over the past 6 months, the CMA’s new consumer enforcement regime has moved firmly into delivery phase. We have secured practical results for consumers while sharpening our focus on the harms and reforms that will shape the year ahead.
Our work so far this year
Since April 2026, we have:
Alongside our investigations, we have also continued our work to promote compliance, including:
Looking ahead

In the months ahead, we will continue to focus on practices that can cause significant consumer harm across markets, including continuing to bear down on drip pricing, misleading time limited offers or fake reviews. But our investigations into Adobe, Euro Car Parks, Ryanair and Microsoft show we are also willing to investigate conduct by individual businesses. We will act on intelligence and where there are problems, we expect businesses to put issues right quickly.
Pricing practices and online choice

We will continue to tackle drip pricing, partition pricing and online designs that obscure the true cost of a purchase or distort consumer choice. We have settled 7 of our 8 original online pricing practice investigations launched in November 2025, most recently Gold’s Gym, Wayfair and Buy It Direct, imposing penalties of over £6,000,000 and securing over £440,000 in consumer redress in these three cases.

Our newer investigations into Virgin Atlantic, Trainline and Red Driving School show that complete, accurate pricing remains a priority so consumers always know the total price that they will pay. We are also reviewing how online retailers disclose delivery fees and expect to provide an update shortly.
Using our intelligence capabilities, we are also watching for businesses who might be using misleading discounts.
Our expectation:

Discounts must be genuine and businesses must show the total price clearly and throughout the purchasing journey, without opting customers in by pre-selecting extra services. Online journeys should support informed choices. The rules are clear, and businesses have had ample time to comply.
Fake and misleading reviews

We continue to progress our investigations into Autotrader, Feefo, Dignity, Just Eat and Pasta Evangelists over concerns that consumer law on misleading reviews may have been broken, and we expect to provide a further update in the coming months. We have provided clear guidance about publishing consumer reviews and complying with consumer protection law.
Our expectation:

Businesses that host or use reviews should have effective systems to prevent misleading content and should act promptly when problems are identified. They should also bear in mind that commissioning reviews can take many forms and isn’t limited to paying consumers for them, for example unlawful conduct could include a business requesting members of staff to write reviews about its products or services.
AI products and services

We are actively monitoring how AI products are marketed and used, working with consumer groups and businesses to identify how benefits can be harnessed as well as emerging risks. Our guidance on using AI agents explains how existing consumer law applies to agentic AI.

In July we also opened an investigation examining concerns about how Microsoft presented information to consumers about changes to Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscriptions, including the addition of new, AI-related features such as Copilot.
Our expectation:
Providers and businesses deploying AI must be responsible and accountable to consumers. New technology does not change their responsibility to comply with consumer law.
Subscription contracts

A new subscription contracts regime will come into force in January to ensure customers are better informed and make it easier for people to cancel plans they no longer want. Ahead of this, the government will be publishing secondary legislation and further guidance.

In the early months of the regime, the CMA’s focus will be on supporting businesses to get this right to help drive the best outcomes for consumers. However, businesses should not assume that our support for compliance means enforcement of the rules is being delayed. Conduct during this period may still be considered as part of enforcement action.

In line with our approach to consumer protection, we will use our powers proportionately by focusing enforcement on more egregious conduct, particularly in areas where businesses should already be clear about their obligations under the existing law. We will consider genuine efforts to comply with the new subscription rules when deciding whether to intervene.
Our expectation:
Businesses will be working to bring themselves into compliance with the new subscription contracts rules as quickly as possible.
Summing up

Over the last 6 months, we have continued to build on the strong foundations laid in the first year of the direct enforcement regime. The first half of this year has shown that our twin approach of helping businesses comply while showing the real consequences for those who don’t is continuing to deliver real benefits for consumers.
