title: From condition to confidence: caring for flood defences in a changing climate

content.content: Behind England’s flood defences are thousands of engineers, inspectors and specialists working in all weathers, around the clock. As Chief Engineer at the Environment Agency, I am proud to lead that effort. This Flood Action Week, we are asking everyone to check whether they are at risk and to know what to do if flooding happens. It is also a good moment to explain how we look after the tens of thousands of flood defences, structures and systems that help keep communities safer, reduce coastal erosion and manage water.
Why we need to keep adapting

We are aware of and listening to the concerns and frustrations of communities. Many flood defences are ageing, and more frequent and severe weather is placing them under greater pressure. It’s important to know that if an asset is below required condition, it does not automatically mean it has failed or stopped protecting people.

Nevertheless, we know the condition of the flood defences we manage because we inspect and monitor them regularly and draw on the knowledge of our local teams. We assess the risk, prioritise the work and put extra checks or other measures in place while repairs are planned or completed.

We have moved more funding into maintenance and targeted repairs and as a result, the proportion of our most important assets meeting the condition we require remained broadly stable at 92–93% through to December 2025.

The message is clear: as the climate changes, the way we care for flood defences must change too. Regular inspections and maintenance remain essential. Better information will also help us spot deterioration earlier and direct funding to the places where it can do most to reduce flood risk.
A fuller picture of how our defences are performing

For more than fifteen years, we have used condition checks as the main way of judging how well flood defences, navigation structures and water-management assets are being looked after. Those checks remain important, but they cannot tell us everything. We are therefore developing a broader approach, called Asset Health, to show not only an asset’s condition but also how well it is likely to perform over time.

Asset Health will give us a clearer, more complete picture of how each asset is performing and the part it plays in protecting a wider area. It will combine what we learn from inspections and monitoring with evidence about how an asset is ageing, what could cause it to fail, what the effects might be and how reliable our information is. This will help us intervene earlier and invest where action can make the greatest difference to homes, businesses, communities and the environment.

By 2028, every asset we manage will have a target health rating based on the role it plays and what would happen if it failed. This will help us make better decisions about when to inspect, maintain, repair or replace an asset—and explain those decisions more clearly to the public.
What's already changing

This is already beginning. We have updated our standards and, over the next few years, will make greater use of technology that can check assets from a distance. This will support—not replace—the regular inspections carried out by our teams and help us spot changes sooner.

For example, laser surveys can measure the shape and height of earth banks, while sensors can send us regular information without waiting for a site visit. These tools will not replace our inspectors, whose expertise and judgement remain essential. They will give inspectors a fuller picture of how assets are changing and provide earlier warning of possible problems.
Innovation with purpose (and proof)
We use innovation where there is clear evidence that it can solve real problems more safely, quickly or affordably.

Targeted support helped Internal Drainage Boards—local public bodies that manage water levels in low-lying areas—repair and upgrade important equipment after the exceptionally wet winter of 2023–24. At Black Sluice in Lincolnshire, funding paid for mobile pumps and the equipment needed to use them. When flooding occurred in January 2025, the team deployed the pumps quickly, helping to reduce the risk to homes, businesses and farmland.

On the Rother Tidal Walls East project, our innovation fund supported the use of a specialist excavator that can work safely on steep or difficult ground. Compared with conventional heavy machinery, this cut project costs by around 40% and potential carbon emissions by approximately 90%. It is a practical example of how tested new approaches can save money, reduce carbon and sustain flood protection.
Learning from the world, leading at home

The Environment Agency is one of many organisations that manage flood risk. In England, drainage boards, councils and landowners also look after flood defences, so working together is essential. We share practical lessons with partners in the UK and overseas—for example, how to maintain movable barriers and how different grasses can strengthen earth banks while supporting nature.
Sharing evidence and experience helps us improve faster, test our assumptions and adopt approaches that have already worked elsewhere.
Flood risk is growing as the climate changes, and many of the structures we rely on are ageing. We are clear about that challenge, and we are acting on it.

We know the condition of the assets we manage and are improving our understanding of how they are ageing. That evidence helps us decide when and where to act. Through sustained maintenance, targeted repairs, better monitoring and close partnership, we will continue to look after these assets so they can keep reducing flood risk for communities into the future.

There will always be more to do, and no flood defence can remove every risk. Managing flood risk is a shared responsibility. During Flood Action Week, our teams will keep inspecting, maintaining and improving defences. Everyone can help by checking their own flood risk, signing up for warnings where available and knowing what to do if flooding happens.
To find out more about how you can protect your home or business this Flood Action Week, visit Flood Action Online.

title: Using AI to analyse legacy systems faster: what our pilots revealed
authors: Joe Ward, Head of Firmer Foundations Strategy & Policy Team | Office of Chief Technology Officer, Digital Transformation Directorate, GDS

content.content: AI can help organisations analyse legacy systems faster
One of the biggest barriers to modernising legacy technology is understanding how existing systems work.

To modernise systems, organisations first need a clear picture of how applications work, connect and depend on one another. That process can take weeks or even months. Documentation is often incomplete or out of date, knowledge may be concentrated in a small number of specialists, and some systems rely on technologies that few engineers still work with regularly.
Our pilots indicate that AI-assisted approaches could help technical teams analyse some legacy systems more quickly.
Across participating organisations, activities estimated to take weeks using traditional approaches were completed in hours.

Working with organisations including the Student Loans Company (SLC), the UK Hydrographic Office (UKHO), the Met Office, and our delivery partner Kainos, we found that AI can help teams analyse unfamiliar systems, identify dependencies and build technical knowledge more quickly than traditional approaches alone. The pilots covered different systems and technical environments, so the results should not be treated as directly applicable to every legacy estate.
However, for organisations managing large and complex technology estates, this could make some modernisation activities easier to prioritise, plan and deliver.
What happened at the Student Loans Company
At the Student Loans Company, teams explored how AI assisted approaches could be used to analyse an estate of 33 applications written in Clojure and support future modernisation planning.
Using traditional approaches, the work was estimated to take around five weeks. During the pilot, teams completed the analysis in less than a day.
The analysis gave the team a clearer view of the 33 applications and their dependencies, which it used to inform migration planning and work towards supported versions of Java.
The most significant finding was not the reduction in effort itself, but the ability to unlock work that had previously been difficult to prioritise.
What happened at the UK Hydrographic Office
At the UK Hydrographic Office, teams focused on a 20-year old desktop application that previously had no automated tests.

AI assisted techniques were used to generate automated tests for the application. Test coverage increased from 0% to 96%, while regression testing that had previously required around 15 days of manual effort was reduced to approximately 30 minutes.
The benefits extended beyond faster testing.

Teams reported greater confidence in making changes to the application safely and maintaining it over time. For many legacy systems, the perceived risk of change can be a barrier to improvement. The pilot indicated that AI-assisted testing could give engineers more evidence when assessing proposed changes.
Why this matters
The examples from SLC and UKHO illustrate a wider challenge facing organisations across the public sector.

Legacy systems often support critical services, but analysing them can be complex and expensive. Teams may spend weeks mapping dependencies, reviewing code and building technical knowledge before they can assess risks or plan change.

The strongest finding from the pilots was that AI can help accelerate this discovery and assessment phase. That may sound modest, but it addresses a critical point where many modernisation efforts slow down or stall.
By helping teams understand systems more quickly, AI assisted approaches can make it easier to:
In short, AI can help organisations spend less time understanding their systems and more time improving them.
AI is not a substitute for good delivery
The pilots also reinforced an important lesson.
AI does not remove the need for good governance, engineering expertise or delivery capability.

Successful outcomes depended on organisations having the right foundations in place, including clear ownership, access to systems and information, experienced technical teams and established delivery processes.
In practice, the pilots showed that AI amplified existing strengths and weaknesses rather than replacing them.

Used well, AI can accelerate analysis, improve visibility of complex systems and help organisations make progress more quickly. Used without appropriate controls, it can amplify existing problems and accelerate poor decision making.
Where AI-assisted analysis may help
The pilots suggest that AI can significantly reduce the effort required to assess complex systems, helping organisations move more quickly from discovery to modernisation.

For organisations managing large and complex technology estates, this can help engineers, architects and delivery teams to identify risks earlier, making modernisation activities easier to plan, justify and deliver.
What happens next
We are continuing to work with organisations using AI assisted approaches to analyse, assess and modernise legacy systems, building on the lessons from these pilots.

Alongside this work, we are developing a playbook of good practice that captures practical approaches, lessons learned and implementation considerations for organisations looking to apply AI to legacy technology challenges. The playbook is currently undergoing user testing, review and approval ahead of publication.
Get involved

If your organisation is exploring AI assisted approaches to analysing, documenting or modernising legacy systems, or would like to share experiences and engage with our wider Firmer Foundations programme, we would like to hear from you. Get in touch at firmer.foundations@dsit.gov.uk

Automated test coverage increased from 0% to 96%, meaning almost all code in a legacy application could be checked automatically before making changes. These findings from our pilots show how AI assisted approaches can help organisations analyse legacy systems faster and modernise them with greater confidence.

title: UK NSC seminar on HPV vaccination and the future of cervical screening

content.content: Well over 200 people joined the latest UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) online seminar.

The event on 30 September focused on high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) vaccination and its potential impact on the future of cervical screening. Attendees joined from a wide array of backgrounds, including screening specialists, clinicians, academics, commercial organisations and charities.
The 4 excellent presentations addressed many questions that had been submitted to the UK NSC inbox ahead of the seminar and they were followed by a busy question and answer session.
As always, there were more questions than time available to answer them in – but anyone with an unanswered query is welcome to send it to us at UKNSC@dhsc.gov.uk.
The presentations
Copies of the presenters’ slides are available via links below.

Philippa Pearmain, from NHS England, presented on the current NHS Cervical Screening Programme. She explained how the programme had developed, spoke about cervical screening uptake rates and covered the introduction of HPV self-sampling for non-responders.

Sharif Ismail, from the UK Health Security Agency, spoke about HPV vaccination in England, the importance of early vaccination, variations in vaccination coverage and how vaccination awareness remains a challenge.

Professor Peter Sasieni, from Queen Mary University London, presented his research on the impact of HPV vaccination. He spoke about how cervical cancer mortality has declined in relation to increased vaccine uptake, and looked at progress towards the elimination of cervical cancer in vaccinated people.

Carolina Martinelli, from the UK NSC evidence team, looked to the future. Carolina covered modelling work being undertaken in Australia and the UK NSC’s exploration of an HPV self-sampling offer to everyone eligible for cervical screening.

title: Inaccurate reporting on Community Recovery Fund

content.content: Several outlets have claimed that Angela Rayner, Secretary of State has provided funding directly to partisan organisations via the Community Recovery Fund. This is not correct.
The facts

Put simply, councils are not permitted to spend taxpayers’ money on partisan issues or party-political activity. They are responsible for ensuring public funding is used appropriately, and action can be taken where spending is found to have breached the relevant requirements. Any suggestion that this was a decision taken by the Secretary of State is not true.
An MHCLG spokesperson said:
“Councils are not permitted to use taxpayers’ money to fund partisan issues or party-political activity.
“Councils must make sure money is spent in line with their responsibilities, and we have powers in place to recoup money if it is found to have been mis-spent.”

title: Beneath the surface: what my award taught me about school finance
authors: Chris Bramall, School Business Manager, The Milford Academy

content.content: Chris Bramall didn't set out to win an award. He set out to fix a school's finances, save money for pupils, and do his job well. Here's what winning taught him about the quiet, invisible work of school business leaders – and why it matters.
School business leaders don't often stop to reflect. There's always another budget, another problem, another deadline.
When I won the Association of Business Leaders in Education (ABLE) School Business Leader Recognition Award for Financial Expertise, it gave me something I didn't expect. The chance to pause.
The problem nobody sees
When I joined my first school, I had no background in education finance. The books were in a mess. Bills were unpaid. The budget was in deficit.
I didn't panic. I got to work.

Within months, I'd turned that deficit into a surplus. I cleared the unpaid bills. I reviewed every contract and every supplier. I found smarter ways to buy what the school needed, saving thousands of pounds.
I also started a breakfast club from nothing. It cost very little to run, but it changed mornings for dozens of children.
None of this made headlines. That's the point.
Why the invisible work matters

I often compare school business leaders to the legs of a swan. Above the water, everything looks calm. Parents see children learning. Staff see resources turn up when needed. Governors see a balanced budget.
Below the water, we're working hard to keep it all moving.

We manage money. We oversee buildings. We support recruitment. We prepare for audits. We solve HR problems. We check contracts. We handle health and safety. Most days bring something we didn't plan for.

When we do our job well, nothing seems to happen. Staff get paid on time. Resources are there when needed. Budgets hold steady. That calm surface is not luck. It's the result of careful, constant work.
What I've learned works
Here's the philosophy that guides me: every pound saved is a pound that can be spent on children.
That means asking one question before every decision: how will this help our pupils?

The lessons from that first school have stayed with me ever since. I’ve looked hard at contracts. I’ve checked every grant we could access. I’ve challenged spending that didn't add value. Wherever I apply them, the same kind of difference starts to follow, usually within months.
This isn't about being clever with spreadsheets, though spreadsheets matter too. It's about treating every pound as if it belongs to a child, because it does.
What the award meant to me
When I found out I'd been shortlisted, my first thought was that plenty of other school business leaders deserved it just as much. That thought didn't go away when I won.
My instinct was to say: "I'm just doing my job."
Then I realised that's exactly what makes this profession special. We don't do this work for recognition. We do it because every decision we make can improve a child's day, or a colleague's.

The award came with a £250 prize for my school. My first thought wasn't about winning something for myself. It was about how that money could help our pupils. I think most school business leaders would say the same.
What I want other school business leaders to know
If you're reading this and thinking, "that's just what I do too," then this is for you.

The work you do beneath the surface is not invisible to the people who benefit from it, even if they never see the effort behind it. Every pound you save. Every contract you improve. Every problem you solve before anyone notices. It all adds up to better outcomes for children.
You don't need an award to know that your work matters. But if the chance comes to be recognised, take it. Not for yourself, but for everyone doing this job quietly, every single day.
Your next step

If you want to see how strong financial leadership could support your school, start with one small thing. Review one contract. Check one supplier. Ask one question: could this pound work harder for our pupils?

Then, if you know a school business leader whose work deserves recognition, nominate them for next year's ABLE School Business Leader Recognition Awards, supported by the Department for Education. Find out more at ablepro.info.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this blog were provided by Chris Bramall and reflect his specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: Designing a digital CAF for local government service

content.content: The Local Digital team is building a digital Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) for local government service to make cyber resilience assessments easier to complete, manage and repeat.

CAF for local government helps councils strengthen their cyber resilience. However, completing, reviewing and repeating assessments can take time. To help make this process simpler, we're developing LG WebCAF, a digital service that will support councils to manage their CAF assessments more easily and consistently over time.
In this blog post, we share:
Your feedback will help us understand how the service works in real conditions and how we can continue to improve it.
Developing LG WebCAF with councils

LG WebCAF will support CAF as a long-term, repeatable approach to assessing and managing cyber resilience. We’re designing the service with councils to make sure it works for the sector’s needs and the realities of teams completing the CAF for local government.

We recently completed the alpha phase. During alpha, we built prototypes of the service and tested them with councils through user research.
This feedback has helped us understand how the service needs to work in practice. We’ve used it to improve the design and focus on what councils need most. This includes:

title: More time and clearer warnings before council tax action 🏠⏰

content.content: New government rules will give people more time to get help with council tax debt – in a shake up that will support people before they face enforcement action.
Here is everything you need to know about what is changing and when.
What is changing? 📰
From April next year:

📬 More warning if you miss a payment: Councils will have to send a reminder and then a final notice before someone who may have missed a payment loses the option to pay in instalments. At the moment, councils only have to send one reminder and can then demand the remaining year’s payment in full.

🗓️ More time to get back on track: To help people get back on track if they have missed a payment, the changes will mean the final notice for council tax payment must be sent at least 14 days after the reminder and at least 41 days after the first missed payment. People will then have another 21 days before losing the option to pay in instalments.

📋 The same clear process, wherever you live: government will also work with councils and debt support organisations to develop guidance and an optional template letter to help make information easier to understand and more consistent, that way everyone knows where they stand with repayment rules.
Other changes to make council tax fairer 📜
🔄 These new rules build on changes already announced to give more protection to households struggling to pay council tax. These include:

🗓️ More time to pay: From April 2027, households will have at least 63 days before they lose the option to pay in instalments. Currently in England, if you miss a monthly payment, councils can, within just three weeks, demand payment for an entire year.
💷 Smaller monthly payments: From April 2028, council tax bills will be spread over 12 months by default instead of 10, making each payment easier to manage.
🤝 More support before debt recovery: Councils will have clear steps to follow and should work with people before taking action to recover unpaid council tax.
Together, these changes will give people who are struggling to pay more time, clearer information and better support before the situation becomes more serious. More details are available here.

title: A royal visit to APHA: Science, conservation and the future of red squirrels

content.content: At APHA, our scientists work on some of the United Kingdom's (UK) most complex wildlife challenges, bringing together expertise from ecology, animal health, engineering and mathematical modelling. Earlier this year, we were delighted to share one such project with a very special visitor when His Majesty The King visited our laboratories at Sand Hutton to learn more about our pioneering research to develop an oral contraceptive for grey squirrels.

The visit provided a valuable opportunity to showcase how science can support conservation and help protect one of Britain's most cherished native species, the red squirrel. As Patron of the Red Squirrel Survival Trust, The King has a real interest in the long-term survival of this native, endangered mammal.
Tackling a long-standing conservation challenge

Red squirrels are an iconic part of the UK's natural heritage, but their populations have declined significantly over the last century. One of the major factors contributing to this decline has been the introduction and spread of the non-native grey squirrel.

Grey squirrels compete with red squirrels for food and habitat and can also carry squirrelpox virus, which has a devastating effect on red squirrel populations. As a result, red squirrels are now largely restricted to a few strongholds across the UK, while grey squirrels remain widespread. Grey squirrels also bark strip young broadleaf trees, negatively affecting woodland ecosystems.

Conservation organisations, land managers and volunteers have worked tirelessly for decades to protect remaining red squirrel populations. At APHA, we are contributing to these efforts through research into innovative, humane and sustainable wildlife management solutions.

One promising area of research, which we have blogged about previously, is the development of fertility control as a tool for population management. Funded by the UK Squirrel Accord and supporters, the current project is working an oral contraceptive specifically designed for grey squirrels. The aim is to reduce grey squirrel populations over time by limiting reproduction, helping to ease pressure on native red squirrels and support woodland biodiversity.
Royal interest in conservation science

During his visit to Sand Hutton, His Majesty met the scientists leading this important programme of work, and representatives of the UK Squirrel Accord providing funding and oversight. The King showed a genuine interest in both the science behind the contraceptive and the challenges associated with translating laboratory research into a practical conservation tool.

Members of the research team discussed the scientific principles underpinning the project, the extensive testing and evaluation required, and the importance of ensuring that any contraceptive delivery system is both effective and species-specific.

The King's thoughtful questions reflected his long-standing interest in environmental issues and wildlife conservation. Throughout the visit, he spent time engaging with scientists from across the programme, learning about the different disciplines contributing to its development.
For our researchers, it was a welcome opportunity to explain how evidence-based science can play a key role in addressing complex ecological challenges and supporting conservation goals.
Innovation beyond the laboratory
Developing an effective wildlife contraceptive requires much more than laboratory science. It also depends on innovative engineering and practical field solutions.

As part of the visit, The King met APHA field workers responsible for designing and testing the bespoke feeding hoppers used to deliver the contraceptive in the field. These specially developed species-specific feeders are a crucial element of the project.

The challenge is to create a system that allows grey squirrels access to the contraceptive bait while minimising access by other wildlife species. Achieving this requires careful design, extensive field testing and continual refinement.

The King's discussions with colleagues highlighted the importance of combining scientific research with practical expertise. From designing feeding systems to monitoring their performance in real-world conditions, every stage of the programme depends on collaboration between specialists from different fields.
Using modelling to understand long-term impacts
The visit also provided an opportunity to showcase the work of APHA's modelling team.

Mathematical modelling plays a vital role in understanding how wildlife populations may respond to different management approaches over time. By analysing data and exploring a range of possible scenarios, researchers can assess the potential long-term effects of the contraceptive programme on squirrel populations and woodland ecosystems.

These models help scientists answer important questions. How quickly might grey squirrel populations respond? What impact could population changes have on red squirrels? How might woodland habitats benefit over time?
By providing evidence-based projections, modelling helps inform decision-making and supports the responsible development of new conservation tools.
The visit provided an opportunity to showcase the value of bringing together multiple scientific disciplines to address environmental challenges.
Recognising the role of volunteers
While science is central to conservation, it is only one part of the picture.

During the visit, His Majesty also met some of the dedicated volunteers who contribute so much to red squirrel conservation efforts across the country. Through monitoring populations, surveying habitats, raising awareness and supporting local conservation initiatives, volunteers play an essential role in protecting red squirrel strongholds.

Their passion, commitment and knowledge have helped sustain conservation programmes over many years. These efforts clearly resonated with The King, who has been a longstanding supporter of red squirrel conservation.
The meeting offered a valuable opportunity to recognise the contribution of the many individuals and organisations working together to safeguard the future of this much-loved species.
A memorable day for APHA
The visit concluded with the unveiling of a commemorative plaque marking the occasion.

As a lasting memento of the day, Erin Thomas, a field ecologist from the APHA Wildlife team, presented His Majesty with a picture of a red squirrel. The gift reflected both the conservation focus of the visit and the dedication of the many people involved in protecting the species.

For everyone involved, the visit was a proud moment and a welcome recognition of the innovative work being carried out at APHA. It also served as a reminder of the importance of collaboration between scientists, field specialists, conservation organisations and volunteers in tackling environmental challenges.

As research into the grey squirrel contraceptive continues, APHA remains committed to developing science-based solutions that support wildlife conservation and help protect the UK's native species. His Majesty's visit provided an invaluable opportunity to highlight this work and to celebrate the dedication of the teams helping to shape a more sustainable future for our natural environment.

In this short video, Bex Pinkham, APHA wildlife biologist, shares an overview of our pioneering grey squirrel contraceptive project and explains how science is helping support the long-term recovery of the UK's native red squirrel population.

title: Engineering quality into digital services
authors: Mibin Boban, Head of Quality Engineering, GDS

content.content: Functional testing can show whether a digital service works as expected, but passing those tests does not on its own mean the service is high quality.
A service can function as expected but still be difficult to use with assistive technology, slow when demand increases, hard to recover when something fails or risky to change.
Quality is shaped by decisions made throughout the life of a service: what we design, how we build, how we release, what we measure and how we respond when something changes.

Building quality in early is not just about reducing defects. It helps teams identify risks when change is easier to make, giving leaders greater confidence and reducing the likelihood of more costly or disruptive problems later.
To help teams think about quality consistently, the cross-government testing community has developed a set of Quality Engineering Principles⁠.
A shared starting point

The creation of the principles started with a workshop bringing together testing and quality engineering practitioners from across government. That conversation highlighted a common challenge: teams were often working towards similar quality outcomes, but we did not have a shared set of principles to describe the approach.
Since then, an active cross-government working group has developed and refined the principles, bringing together experience from different organisations, services and delivery contexts.

We have brought that work together into seven Quality Engineering Principles. These principles set out a shared approach: engineer quality into the way we provide services, take a holistic view of quality, define it around user needs and outcomes, apply effort proportionate to risk, automate repeatable activities, shorten feedback loops and use evidence to make quality measurable, visible and actionable.

The principles are currently in alpha, which means they are a starting point and will continue to evolve. We want teams across government and the wider public sector to try them in real work, challenge them and help us improve them. You can share feedback and suggest improvements directly through the GitHub space.
Quality is more than whether something works

Functional correctness matters, but it is only one part of quality. For a public service, quality can also mean being accessible, secure, resilient and efficient. It should be easy to operate, maintain and change safely. The characteristics that matter most will depend on the service, its users and the consequences if something goes wrong.

This changes the question teams need to ask. Instead of starting with ‘What testing do we need?’, we can start with: ‘What does quality mean for our users and this service, and what evidence will give us confidence that we are achieving it?’. Then teams must consider the wider technical and operational characteristics needed to support them.

For leaders and service owners, this means creating the conditions for teams to make good quality decisions: being clear about the outcomes that matter, understanding risk, and using evidence to know where attention and investment are needed.
Quality is created across the team

Many decisions that determine service quality are not testing decisions. Product teams decide which outcomes matter most. Designers influence usability and accessibility. Engineering and architecture choices affect reliability, security, performance and how easily a service can change. Operational practices determine how quickly teams can detect and recover from problems. Quality engineers bring expertise in areas such as risk analysis, test design, automation and assurance.

Quality engineering therefore works best as part of multidisciplinary delivery. These principles are a way to take the quality conversation beyond testing and quality engineering. They give the wider digital and data community a shared language for thinking about quality and reinforce that it is shaped by decisions across the whole team.
Get useful feedback earlier and more often

One of the strongest ways to improve those decisions is to shorten the time between making a change and learning about its effect. That feedback might come from automated tests, accessibility checks, security controls, performance testing, monitoring, operational data or what we learn from users.

Automation helps where activities are repeatable and where automating them provides value. But automation itself is not the outcome. The outcome is useful feedback at the point where people can act on it.

The same applies to measurement. More dashboards and metrics do not automatically create confidence. Evidence needs to help teams understand whether a service is healthy, where risks are increasing and whether it is providing the outcomes users need.
Apply effort where it matters most

Building quality into delivery does not mean applying the same controls to every change. Different services and changes carry different risks. Teams should consider factors such as complexity, the likelihood of failure and the potential effect on users or the service. Testing and assurance can then be proportionate to that risk. This helps concentrate effort where it provides the most value and confidence rather than creating unnecessary gates.
What happens next

Our aim is to make quality decisions more deliberate, evidence-led and focused on the people who rely on our services. The principles are now available for feedback, and we want to learn from how teams use them in practice. Share your feedback and suggested improvements through the GitHub space. We’ll review what we hear, refine the principles where needed and share updates as they evolve.

description: The cross-government testing community’s Quality Engineering Principles have been developed to help teams build quality throughout the lifecycle of a digital service.

title: Avoidable requisitions continue to fall as we work together
authors: Andrew Robertson, Head of Customer Policy

content.content: At a glance
A shared achievement

Avoidable requisitions have fallen substantially since 2022. We would like to thank conveyancers, post-completion teams, industry bodies and HM Land Registry caseworkers for the time, care and commitment that have made this possible.

Fewer avoidable requisitions is good news for professional customers, their clients and HM Land Registry. It means fewer delays, less additional work and a smoother application process. Conveyancers can spend less time resolving past issues that could have been prevented and more time progressing new transactions for their clients.
It also frees up HM Land Registry caseworkers to process more applications more quickly and to focus on the genuinely challenging issues in registration law.

A requisition is a request for more information or action. A single requisition may contain more than one avoidable point, covering separate errors or omissions that could usually have been prevented before submission. This is why we sometimes refer to avoidable points when describing the data.
Common avoidable requisition points include name discrepancies, identity evidence errors, unclear plans or missing supporting documents.

Avoidable requisition points fell year on year between 2022 and 2025. By 2025, we were raising 400,000 fewer per year than in 2022. Annual totals fell from 839,000 in 2022 to 439,000 in 2025 - a reduction of 47.7%. Application volumes also changed during the same period, but even after adjusting for this, the number of avoidable points relative to application intake fell by 39.1%. This shows that most of the improvement came from fewer avoidable points per application, rather than simply from a change in workload.

And the positive trend continues. Between January and September 2026, there were around 94 avoidable requisition points per 1,000 applications, 11% fewer than in 2025 and almost half (46%) the number in 2022.
Why the improvement matters

Submitting complete and correct applications saves time across the property transaction and registration process. In 2025, around 400,000 fewer avoidable requisition points were raised than in 2022. We estimate this represents a saving of around £12 million in industry time spent resolving preventable issues.

How did we reach that figure? When we began talking more widely about avoidable requisitions in 2022 and 2023, it became clear that the number of avoidable points alone did not fully show their practical impact on conveyancing firms.

To help make the scale of the issue more tangible, HM Land Registry economists and data analysts developed an indicative cost benchmark. Using published sector pay rates and an estimate of the staff time involved, they calculated an indicative cost of up to £31.42 per point. We first used this benchmark in our 2024 blog, The Scale and Cost of Requisitions, to illustrate the potential impact on the industry.

Applying the same benchmark to the latest figures provides a consistent comparison. It is not a calculation of the actual saving made by individual firms: costs will vary according to who handles the work and how long it takes. The benchmark is based on 2023 pay data and has not been adjusted for inflation, so it may understate the equivalent cost today.

The improvement does, however, reflect action across the sector, and we would like to thank everyone who has contributed. Conveyancers and post-completion teams have strengthened checks, reviewed their requisition data and made use of training and guidance. Industry bodies have helped share good practice and raise awareness. HM Land Registry has introduced more digital checks, while caseworkers and support teams have continued to improve how requisitions are raised.

Internal checks show that fewer cases now involve an unnecessary requisition or one where the recorded reason did not accurately reflect the issue. Together, these quality issues affected 12% of checked cases in 2022/23, falling to 10% in 2024/25 and 8% in 2025/26. This suggests that internal checks, guidance and learning are helping caseworkers raise the right requisitions more consistently.
What has helped

There is no single reason for the fall. Better use of data, stronger checks before submission – including digital checks, more targeted training and support, and continued attention to application quality have all played a part.

Customers can use the free webinars, videos and learning resources on HM Land Registry’s training hub to help prevent common errors. For our part, we will continue to improve guidance and training, strengthen internal practice, implement digital checks and help caseworkers raise the right requisition, record it accurately and explain it clearly.
Next: turning progress into practical action

The overall picture is encouraging, but some avoidable requisition reasons remain much more common than others. In Part 2, we focus on the highest-impact issues, the checks that can prevent them and what HM Land Registry will do to support further improvement.

description: Avoidable requisitions have fallen by more than 47% since 2022. In the first of two blogs, we look at what the latest data tells us, how HM Land Registry and its customers are working together and why the progress is not simply the result of fewer applications.

title: New funding backs innovative satellite projects to grow the UK’s climate services sector

content.content: The UK Space Agency is backing seven new projects that will use satellite data to help organisations understand, manage and respond to climate risks, supporting the continued growth of the UK’s climate services sector.

Funded through the Commercial Climate Services Call 4 with a combined investment of £500,000, the seven projects will develop practical, market-focused services that turn Earth observation data into insights for housing providers, investors, infrastructure owners, planners, farmers and public health decision-makers.

The latest call builds on the UK Space Agency’s work to help organisations transform satellite-derived information into commercial services that support economic growth, climate adaptation and national resilience.

Climate change is creating new risks for communities, infrastructure, industry and nature. The successful projects show how UK organisations are using space data to build services that help customers make better decisions, target investment and plan for the future.
Beth Greenaway, UK Space Agency’s Head of Earth Observation Delivery, said:
Each of the seven projects will bring together satellite data, climate science and commercial insight to address real-world challenges:

Quantum Risk Solutions is developing Home Horizon so that social landlords can identify, before the next heatwave, which of their homes are most at risk of becoming dangerously hot. The service uses satellite thermal and optical data plus open building records to rank every home in a landlord's stock by heat risk. With Awaab's Law extending to excess heat from November 2026, it helps landlords protect their most vulnerable residents and proactively invest limited improvement budgets where the need is greatest.

WieldMore, an FCA-authorised firm specialising in climate risk, is developing CERES (Comprehensive Environmental Risk Evaluation System)-Horizon to turn satellite Earth Observation data and climate projections into asset-level measures of climate adaptation and resilience. The service will help investors, including pension funds, and owners of renewable, industrial, agricultural and digital infrastructure understand how physical climate risk affects future cashflows, stress-test existing assets and candidate sites, and quantify the adaptation capex needed to reduce future losses. By linking climate science directly to financial models, CERES-Horizon will help identify where each pound invested in adaptation can protect the greatest amount of long-term asset value.

Frontierra in partnership with ZSL will develop a new satellite-powered water intelligence service that provides asset-level insight into changing water availability. By turning Earth Observation data into actionable risk intelligence for investors and asset owners, the project will identify water-related vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and industrial assets, including hydropower and data centres. Pilots with leading financial institutions and corporates will validate the service, supporting more resilient investment and adaptation decisions as climate change increases pressure on water resources.

Callala Ltd, together with the University of Strathclyde, is developing PEEPS (Platform Environmental Evidence & Performance Sentinel), an Earth observation service for offshore oil and gas platforms. Emissions reporting from these platforms currently relies on operators' own disclosures. PEEPS will use satellite-derived nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) measurements to provide independent evidence of their environmental performance. Building on the university's existing research, it will score and benchmark platforms against their peers, flag those whose emissions differ materially, and link each one to its operator and parent company over time. The aim is investment-grade evidence that helps responsible investors, lenders and insurers work with companies to drive operational change. Further, it is a step towards independent verification of wider greenhouse gas reporting.

SpaceD is using satellite thermal data to measure the effects data centres can have regarding urban heat, a growing risk as UK cities face more frequent heatwaves. Built into SpaceD's siting platform, this evidence will help planners, local authorities and data centre developers choose better sites and grow the UK's digital infrastructure without adding to local climate risk.

Agtelligence is tackling the lack of trusted, farm-level climate and sustainability data in agricultural supply chains by developing FarmScore, a satellite-derived scoring service for coffee farms. By combining Earth observation with AI, FarmScore gives lenders, insurers and buyers a consistent, verifiable view of deforestation risk, land-use change and climate exposure for individual farms. Through commercialisation with agri-finance partners and expansion into traceability for the wider agri community, the service will help direct capital towards more resilient, sustainable farming and support compliance with regulations such as the EU Deforestation Regulation.

Golden Mile Research and Consultancy Ltd’s Compound Heat Air Quality Forecasting Service (CHAQFS) combines air quality and heat exposure data with public health information to develop a predictive tool that forecasts respiratory health risk from the combined effects of heat and air pollution. CHAQFS will support earlier public health interventions, better-informed planning decisions, and stronger climate adaptation strategies.
Supporting a world-leading climate services economy

By supporting these projects, the UK Space Agency is helping companies and research organisations move promising ideas closer to market, attract investment and create services that can be used by customers in the UK and internationally.

The Commercial Climate Services Call is part of the UK Space Agency’s wider commitment to strengthen the Earth observation sector and demonstrate how space can support better decisions on the ground. As demand for trusted climate information grows, these new projects will help ensure the UK remains at the forefront of turning satellite data into practical, commercial services.

description: The UK Space Agency is backing seven new projects that will use satellite data to help organisations better respond to climate risks, supporting the continued growth of the UK’s climate services sector.

title: Beating the beetle: Ips typographus eradicated from 2022 outbreak sites

content.content: Following the successful eradication of the eight-toothed spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus) from all 13 outbreak sites identified in 2021, I’m pleased to confirm that the majority of the 2022 outbreak sites found in south-east England have also been successfully cleared of this destructive pest. This is really positive news for our trees, woods and forests.

As Head of Plant Health Forestry, I lead on the operational work to detect and manage tree health issues, as well as mitigating plant pest and disease risks. In this blog, I’ll explain what this success means for you and your woodland, and how you can help reduce the risks from this pest.
Removing Ips typographus from 2022 sites

Back in 2022, 16 outbreaks of Ips typographus were found at woodland sites across Kent and Sussex, due to wind-assisted incursions of the beetle from continental Europe where it is endemic. Since then, these sites have been subject to robust management action and monitoring in line with international protocols. This requires 3 years of trapping and surveillance following the removal of infested spruce trees and those in close proximity.

We've successfully eradicated Ips typographus from 13 of the 16 sites following this process. Eradication means the elimination of breeding populations at individual outbreak sites. Thorough site walkovers have found no infested material, giving us confidence that the pest has been fully eradicated from these sites.

The remaining 3 sites will need some extra attention due to the existence of residual material after initial clearance work. As a precautionary measure, we have decided to extend our pheromone trapping at these 3 sites for another year. As no active breeding populations have been identified, eradication is expected to be confirmed at these sites next year.
Why eradication matters

Eradicating breeding populations of Ips typographus at individual outbreak sites shows that our policy approach and operational activity – led by the Forestry Commission, Forest Research and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs – is working to prevent this pest from establishing in England.

We are very encouraged that our world-leading programme has successfully eradicated the eight-toothed spruce bark beetle from the majority of 2022 outbreak sites, building on the successful eradication of the 2018 and 2021 outbreak sites.

However, there’s a wider concern that's relevant to all woodland owners. With a changing climate, we’re seeing an ever-increasing risk from pests and diseases. This requires a huge effort by the Plant Health Service to mitigate risks and take action if outbreaks occur.

Spruce trees are vitally important to the UK's timber security, but warmer and more extreme weather increases the risk of trees becoming stressed and more vulnerable to Ips typographus, particularly in higher risk areas such as the south and east of England.
An encouraging trend
Alongside the successful eradication of the 2021 outbreak sites and most sites identified in 2022, our robust surveillance programme continues to detect new outbreaks at a very early stage.

Most sites involve low-level infestations, with small pioneering breeding populations and low beetle numbers. This is encouraging and demonstrates that our integrated approach, combining pheromone trapping, aerial surveillance and ground inspections, are helping us to find outbreaks early, when eradication measures are most effective.
However, there is no room for complacency. Ips typographus continues to arrive from continental Europe, with new outbreaks detected and managed each year following wind-assisted incursions.

While most outbreaks are small and localised, their detection reflects the strength of our surveillance programme and our ability to respond rapidly. Continued vigilance from woodland owners and managers, alongside extensive trapping, aerial surveillance and ground inspections, remains essential to protect UK forestry.
How you can help beat the beetle
There's a role for every spruce woodland owner to play. It’s important to:
Working together to prevent Ips typographus establishment
The fight against Ips typographus will require continued effort and vigilance from everyone involved.

If you’d like to get more directly involved, you can join the national monitoring project run by Forest Research, Forestry Commission and the Sylva Foundation. If you own or manage woodland with spruce in England, Wales or Scotland, you can volunteer to host a bark beetle trap and help collect samples. It's a great way to become part of the early warning system that helps us catch outbreaks before they take hold.
If you own woodland with spruce in the proactive spruce removal area, financial support is available to help you manage your woodlands to reduce risk. Available grants include:
Proactive spruce management can reduce the risk of the pest, protect tree health and woodland value, maximise timber production and give you greater flexibility and time to plan.
If you own or manage a spruce woodland, please keep checking the health of your trees, report anything unusual and make use of the support and grants on offer.
Early detection and management are essential to prevent outbreaks. Together, we can help prevent this destructive pest from establishing and protect our trees, woodlands and forests.

description: Andrea Deol, Head of Plant Health Forestry at the Forestry Commission, shares the successful eradication of Ips typographus from 13 outbreak sites and how to help prevent future establishment.
